title: Brake fluid leak
h1: Is my car leaking brake fluid?
metaDesc: Think your car is leaking brake fluid? Check the pedal, the warning light and where the fluid is to see how serious it is and what your mechanic should check.
synonyms: brake pedal soft and leaking fluid
is it safe to drive with a brake fluid leak
intro: Brake fluid is clear to yellowish when new and turns amber or brown with age. It feels slick, like light oil, and has little smell. Because your brakes depend on it, a real brake fluid leak means the car shouldn't be driven, so we'll start with how the brakes feel.
safety: If the brake pedal sinks toward the floor, don't drive the car.

If the pedal sinks or goes to the floor while you're driving, turn on your hazard lights, keep pressing the brake, shift to a lower gear, and pull the parking brake on gradually. Steer toward an open, safe area. Once stopped, don't drive it again; have it towed.
If the red BRAKE light stays on with the parking brake released, don't drive the car.

q_pedal.q: How does the brake pedal feel?
q_pedal.help: Press it firmly with the engine running and the car in Park. A healthy pedal stops high and feels firm.

opts.a: Soft or spongy, or it slowly sinks toward the floor
The red BRAKE warning light is on
Firm and normal, and no brake warning light

q_light.q: With the engine running and the parking brake fully released, is the red BRAKE light on?
q_light.help: It may say BRAKE or show a circle with an exclamation mark. It also comes on when the parking brake is set, so release that first.

q_where.q: Where did you find the fluid?

opts.a: On the inside of a wheel or tire
Along a metal line or rubber hose under the car
Under the hood, around the brake fluid reservoir near the windshield
On the floor inside the car, under the pedals
I haven't seen a leak, but the fluid level looks low

q_level.q: Look at the brake fluid reservoir under the hood. Where is the level?
q_level.help: It's a see-through plastic tank, usually on the driver's side near the windshield, marked MIN and MAX. You can read it without opening the cap. Brake fluid damages paint, so wipe up any drips right away.

opts.a: At or near MAX, and I see no wet spots anywhere
Between the lines but closer to MIN, and I see no wet spots
At or below MIN, or empty

result.title: The brakes may be losing pressure. Don't drive the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the pedal sinks while you're driving, keep pressing the brake, turn on your hazard lights, apply the parking brake gradually and steer to a safe stop.
If you can't find any outside leak, a master cylinder leaking internally can cause the same sinking pedal. It still needs a tow.
result.why: A soft or sinking pedal means the brake system can't hold pressure, because fluid is escaping or air has gotten in. Together with a leak, this means braking could fail. The car isn't safe to use until it's repaired.

causes.name: Leak at a caliper, wheel cylinder, line or hose
causes.clues: Wet fluid near a wheel or along the underside of the car.

causes.name: Master cylinder problem
causes.clues: The pedal slowly sinks while you hold steady pressure, with or without a visible leak.

causes.name: Air in the brake lines
causes.clues: Recent brake work, or the reservoir ran very low.

shop: Brake line, hose and caliper inspection
Brake bleed and pedal test after repair

result.title: The red brake light with a leak can point to low brake fluid
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the parking brake was partly on, release it fully and look again. Even if the light goes out, have the suspected leak checked before using the car.
If the ABS light is also on, mention it. Some brake faults turn on both.
result.why: The red brake light comes on when the parking brake is set or when the fluid in the reservoir drops too low. With a leak, low fluid is the likely reason, and the next stage can be a pedal that sinks to the floor.

causes.name: Low fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Wet spots near a wheel or under the car, or a reservoir at or below MIN.

causes.name: Very worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, and a long time since the last brake job.
causes.against: Pad wear alone rarely drops the level fast enough to explain fresh drips.

causes.name: Faulty fluid level sensor or parking brake switch
causes.clues: The reservoir is full and there's no sign of a leak.

you: Make sure the parking brake is fully released.
Look at the brake fluid reservoir level without opening it.
shop: Brake fluid level and leak inspection

result.title: Brake fluid may be leaking at a wheel (caliper or wheel cylinder)
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If fluid has soaked the brake pads or shoes, a shop will usually replace them as well. Contaminated pads don't grip properly.
If it turns out to be thick black grease instead of slick fluid, it may be a torn axle boot. Still have it checked before using the car.
result.why: Each wheel has a caliper, or a wheel cylinder on drum brakes, that uses brake fluid to press the pads or shoes. A leak there drains fluid and can coat the pads, so that wheel brakes poorly. The pedal can go soft with little warning.

causes.name: Caliper piston seal leaking
causes.clues: Wet, slick fluid on the inside of a front wheel.

causes.name: Leaking wheel cylinder (drum brakes)
causes.clues: Wetness on the inside of a rear tire, on a car with rear drum brakes.

causes.name: Loose bleeder screw or brake hose fitting
causes.clues: The leak started after recent brake work.

you: Without driving the car, look at the inside of each tire for a wet, oily film.

result.title: A brake line or hose may be leaking
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the lines look heavily rusted, ask the shop to inspect all of them, not just the leaking section.
result.why: Brake lines carry fluid under high pressure to each wheel. Steel lines rust from road salt, and rubber hoses crack with age. A leaking line can burst when you brake hard, causing a sudden loss of braking.

causes.name: Rusted steel brake line
causes.clues: An older car driven in snowy, salted areas, with flaky rust along the lines.

causes.name: Cracked or worn rubber brake hose
causes.clues: Wetness at the flexible hose near a wheel, or visible cracks.

causes.name: Loose fitting
causes.clues: Fluid at a connection, especially after recent brake work.

shop: Full brake line and hose inspection on a lift

result.title: Brake fluid may be leaking from the main brake pump near the pedal (master cylinder)
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If it's only old, dried residue from a past top-up and the level holds steady, a technician can confirm that and clear the car to use.
If your car is a manual, the clutch often shares this fluid. Mention it if the clutch pedal also feels different.
result.why: The master cylinder turns your foot pressure into brake fluid pressure. If it leaks outside or its seals fail inside, the pedal can sink and braking power drops. Brake fluid also eats paint, so bubbled or peeling paint below it is a clue.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder seal or line fitting
causes.clues: Fresh wetness below the master cylinder, or peeling paint underneath.

causes.name: Cracked reservoir or loose cap
causes.clues: Wetness around the reservoir itself.

causes.name: Spill from an earlier top-up
causes.clues: Dry residue, and the level stays the same over several days.
causes.against: Fresh wetness that returns after the area is cleaned points to a real leak.

you: Note whether the area looks freshly wet or just has old residue.
Look at the reservoir level without opening it.

result.title: Fluid under the pedals could be from the brake or clutch system
result.now: Don't drive it until it's checked. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If it's plain water or smells sweet, it may be an A/C drain or heater core leak instead. Still have the brake fluid level and pedal checked before driving, and mention any sweet smell or foggy windows to the shop.

If the car is a manual and the clutch pedal feels soft or sticks, the clutch system may be the source. Many cars share the brake fluid reservoir with the clutch, so it still needs checking before you drive.
result.why: The brake master cylinder, and on manual cars the clutch master cylinder, sit just in front of the pedals. A leak there can run back toward the pedal area. Both use brake fluid, and many cars share one reservoir, so either leak can lead to low brake fluid.

causes.name: Leaking clutch master cylinder (manual cars)
causes.clues: A soft, sticking or sinking clutch pedal.

causes.name: Leaking brake master cylinder or pushrod seal
causes.clues: A soft or sinking brake pedal, and the brake fluid level dropping.

causes.name: Water or coolant
causes.clues: Plain water, or a sweet smell and foggy windows.
causes.against: Brake fluid is slick and has little smell.

you: Touch a drop: slick and nearly odorless suggests brake or clutch fluid, watery or sweet suggests water or coolant.
Look at the brake fluid reservoir level without opening it.
shop: Brake and clutch master cylinder inspection

result.title: Low brake fluid with no obvious cause should be treated as a leak
result.now: Don't drive it until a technician has checked the brakes. Have it towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If the brakes were worked on recently, ask that shop to check for a loose fitting or bleeder screw first.
If the brake pads turn out to be worn almost through, that can explain part of the drop, but the pads need replacing right away.
result.why: The brake system is sealed, and the fluid level only drops slightly as pads wear. At or below MIN means very worn pads or fluid escaping somewhere you can't see, and braking can fail if it keeps dropping.

causes.name: Hidden leak at a caliper, line or hose
causes.clues: Damp areas on the inside of a wheel or along the underside.

causes.name: Very worn brake pads
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, and a long time since the last brake job.

causes.name: Master cylinder leaking into the brake booster
causes.clues: No outside leak, but the level keeps dropping and the pedal feels different.

you: Without driving the car, look at the inside of each tire for a wet film.

result.title: The fluid you found may not be brake fluid, but have the brakes checked
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days so a shop can identify the fluid and confirm the brakes aren't leaking. Check the reservoir again before each drive until then.
if: If the brake fluid level drops when you check again, treat it as a leak and don't drive the car until it's checked.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the red BRAKE light comes on, the car pulls to one side when braking, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
result.why: A full reservoir and a firm pedal are good signs, but they don't prove there's no leak. A slow leak can take time to lower the level. Other fluids near the wheels, like shock absorber oil or axle grease, can also look similar.

causes.name: Leaking shock absorber or strut
causes.clues: An oily film on the shock body behind the wheel, and a bouncier ride.

causes.name: Torn CV axle boot
causes.clues: Thick black grease sprayed around the inside of a front wheel.

causes.name: Power steering or other fluid
causes.clues: Reddish or amber fluid toward the front of the car.

you: Recheck the brake fluid level in a few days.
Look at the shocks behind each wheel for an oily film.
shop: Shock, strut and axle boot inspection
Brake inspection to rule out a leak

result.title: The level may be dropping as the brake pads wear, but a leak needs to be ruled out
result.now: Have the brakes inspected within the next few days. A shop will usually check pad thickness and look for leaks before deciding whether it's just pad wear. Don't top it up to MAX yourself before the inspection, as the level helps them judge.
if: If the level keeps dropping between checks, or you spot any wet areas near the wheels, treat it as a leak and don't drive the car until it's checked.
If the level reaches MIN or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If the pedal feels soft or sinks, the red BRAKE light comes on, the car pulls to one side when braking, or you smell burning from a wheel, don't drive it until the brakes are checked.
If you hear grinding when you brake, the pads may be worn down to metal. Don't drive it until they're checked.
result.why: As brake pads wear thinner, the brake pistons sit further out and hold more fluid, so the reservoir level drops slowly over many months. That can be normal. A sudden drop, or any dampness near the wheels, is not, and from here it isn't possible to tell the two apart.

causes.name: Brake pad wear
causes.clues: A slow drop over months, and the pads are getting old.

causes.name: Slow leak not yet visible
causes.clues: The level drops noticeably within weeks.

you: Note the level and check it again in a couple of weeks.
Listen for squealing from the brakes, a common pad wear warning.

result.title: Treat it as a brake leak until someone checks
result.now: Don't drive it until a technician has checked the brakes. A mechanic can come to you, or have it towed.
if: If the technician finds the reservoir full, the pedal firm and no leak, the fluid was probably something else.
result.why: Without knowing whether the brake fluid is low or the warning light is on, it isn't possible to rule out a brake leak. Because brakes can fail suddenly when fluid runs low, it's safer to have them checked before using the car.

causes.name: Brake fluid leak
causes.clues: Slick, clear to brown fluid near a wheel or under the car.

causes.name: Another fluid near the wheels
causes.clues: Shock oil, axle grease or power steering fluid.

you: Take a photo of the fluid and where you found it to show the technician.
shop: Brake fluid level and leak inspection
